title: Rights and Responsibilities Where We Live
summary: Map the public places in your own community where people use the rights in the Bill of Rights and carry out their responsibilities as citizens, and find who represents your district in Congress.
subject: History
studentLogin: Not needed to explore the map

layers.name: Congressional districts (119th Congress)
layers.shows: District boundaries for the 119th Congress (2025–2027) as blue outlines, current as of the layer's last update (see its item page); representatives change at elections and in special elections. Each pop-up reads "[Representative Name] ([Party]) represents [State] Congressional District [number]".
layers.source: Esri; U.S. Census Bureau; Clerk of the U.S. House of Representatives (MapMaker catalogue)

layers.name: National Register of Historic Places
layers.shows: Places on the National Register as diamonds colored by type: building, structure, district, site or object. They appear when you zoom in. Each pop-up gives the address, city, county and state, and a link to the National Archives record, but not the place's name; read the name from the basemap label or the National Archives record.

knownIssues.where: National Register of Historic Places pop-up
knownIssues.note: The pop-up shows the address, city, county and state but not the place's name: the Resource Name field (RESNAME) is hidden, so students see an address without a name. Being raised with the MapMaker team. Until it is fixed, students can follow the pop-up's National Archive Information link for the name, or read the name off the Topographic basemap when the building is labeled.

compellingQuestion.en: Where in our community do people use their rights and carry out their responsibilities?
compellingQuestion.es: ¿Dónde, en nuestra comunidad, las personas ejercen sus derechos y cumplen sus responsabilidades?

questions.task: Students zoom to their town on the Topographic basemap and click inside their congressional district to read the pop-up, which names the representative, their party and the district number. Then they zoom out to the whole state and count the blue-outlined districts.
frontOfClass: Zoom to your town on the Topographic basemap until its name shows.
Point out the blue lines: the boundaries of congressional districts.
Click inside the district and read the pop-up.
Ask: who represents us in the House, which party do they belong to, and what is the district's number?
Zoom out until the whole state is on screen.
Ask: how many districts does our state have?

steps.en: Zoom to your town; the basemap has place names.
steps.es: Acércate a tu pueblo o ciudad; el mapa base tiene nombres de lugares.

steps.en: Find the blue lines, which are the boundaries of congressional districts.
steps.es: Busca las líneas azules, que son los límites de los distritos del Congreso.

steps.en: Click inside your district and read the pop-up.
steps.es: Haz clic dentro de tu distrito y lee la ventana emergente.

steps.en: Zoom out to see your whole state.
steps.es: Aléjate para ver todo tu estado.

ask.en: Who represents your district in the House of Representatives, which party do they belong to, and what is the district's number? How many districts does your state have?
ask.es: ¿Quién representa a tu distrito en la Cámara de Representantes, a qué partido pertenece y qué número tiene el distrito? ¿Cuántos distritos tiene tu estado?

answer.where: Congressional districts (119th Congress) pop-up: "[Representative Name] ([Party]) represents [State] Congressional District [number]". The district count is the number of blue-outlined areas in the state when zoomed out, which equals the state's House seats after the 2020 census: for example California 52, Texas 38, Florida 28; six states (Alaska, Delaware, North Dakota, South Dakota, Vermont and Wyoming) have one, shown as the whole state.
answer.accept: Accept the name and party as the pop-up gives them for the 119th Congress (2025–2027); a seat that has changed hands since the layer was updated may differ. In California, Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee, Texas and Utah the district on the November 2026 ballot may differ from the one shown (see the map's description).

questions.task: Students zoom in on their town until the Topographic basemap labels buildings, pick four public places it shows or that they know (courthouse, city hall, library, place of worship, polling place, newspaper office), sketch a pin on each and label it with a right from the Bill of Rights that people use there. Sketches are not saved, so students finish in one session or take a screenshot.
frontOfClass: Zoom in on the town until the basemap labels buildings.
Find one public building the basemap labels, such as a courthouse, city hall or library.
Open Sketch, put a pin on it and add a text label.
Ask: which right from the Bill of Rights do people use here?
Remind the class that sketches are not saved: finish today or take a screenshot.

steps.en: Zoom in on your town until the basemap shows building names.
steps.es: Acércate a tu pueblo o ciudad hasta que el mapa base muestre nombres de edificios.

steps.en: Find four public places, not homes: a courthouse, city hall, library, place of worship, polling place or newspaper office.
steps.es: Encuentra cuatro lugares públicos, no viviendas: un tribunal, el ayuntamiento, una biblioteca, un lugar de culto, un centro de votación o la redacción de un periódico.

steps.en: Use Sketch to put a pin on each one.
steps.es: Usa Sketch (dibujar) para colocar un marcador en cada uno.

steps.en: Next to each pin, write a right from the Bill of Rights that people use there.
steps.es: Junto a cada marcador, escribe un derecho de la Carta de Derechos que las personas ejercen allí.

steps.en: Finish in one lesson or take a screenshot, because sketches are not saved.
steps.es: Termina en una sola clase o toma una captura de pantalla, porque los dibujos no se guardan.

ask.en: Which four places did you pin, and which right from the Bill of Rights do people use at each?
ask.es: ¿Qué cuatro lugares marcaste y qué derecho de la Carta de Derechos ejercen las personas en cada uno?

answer.where: The Topographic basemap labels schools, churches, courthouses, libraries and city halls in most towns at close zoom. Sketch tool: a pin and a text label at each place. There is no stored answer; the teacher checks the student's screen or screenshot.
answer.accept: Four pins on public places (not homes), each paired with a right that fits: a newspaper office with freedom of the press, a place of worship with free exercise of religion, city hall or a public square with assembly and petition, a library with speech and the press, a courthouse with due process or a jury trial (Fifth, Sixth and Seventh Amendments). A polling place connects with voting, which later amendments protect (15th, 19th and 26th), so accept it with that note.

questions.task: Students start from the courthouse or city hall they pinned in question 2, add pins for places where people carry out responsibilities as citizens (voting, jury service, paying taxes), and sort the responsibilities into required by law and voluntary.
frontOfClass: Return to the courthouse or city hall pinned in question 2.
Add a Sketch pin and write next to it the responsibility people carry out there.
Ask: where else in town do people vote, serve on a jury or pay taxes?
Ask: which of these responsibilities are required by law, and which are voluntary?

steps.en: Start at the courthouse or city hall you pinned.
steps.es: Empieza en el tribunal o el ayuntamiento que marcaste.

steps.en: Add a pin at each place where people carry out a citizen's responsibility: voting, jury service, paying taxes.
steps.es: Añade un marcador en cada lugar donde las personas cumplen una responsabilidad ciudadana: votar, formar parte de un jurado, pagar impuestos.

steps.en: Next to each pin, write the responsibility.
steps.es: Junto a cada marcador, escribe la responsabilidad.

ask.en: Which of these responsibilities are required by law, and which are voluntary?
ask.es: ¿Cuáles de estas responsabilidades exige la ley y cuáles son voluntarias?

answer.where: Sketch pins on the student's map, usually at the courthouse (jury service), a polling place such as a school, library or church (voting), and a post office or tax office (paying taxes). There is no stored answer; check the screen or screenshot.
answer.accept: At least two pins with a responsibility each, and a sort that puts obeying laws, paying taxes, jury service when called and, for most men aged 18 through 25, Selective Service registration under required by law, and voting, staying informed, volunteering and attending community meetings under voluntary. Accept the point that voting is both a right and a responsibility, but no federal law requires it.

questions.task: Turn on National Register of Historic Places, zoom in until the diamonds appear, and click the two nearest the school. The pop-up gives the address but not the name, so students match the diamond to the basemap label or follow the pop-up's National Archive Information link. Look for a public building and the right or responsibility it connects with.
frontOfClass: In Map layers, turn on National Register of Historic Places.
Zoom in near the school until the diamonds appear.
Open the legend and show the diamond colors for building, district and site.
Click the diamond nearest the school and read the address in the pop-up.
Match it to the basemap label, or open the pop-up's National Archive Information link for the name.
Ask: is it a public building, and which right or responsibility does it connect with?

steps.en: In Map layers, turn on National Register of Historic Places.
steps.es: En las capas del mapa (Map layers), activa National Register of Historic Places (Registro Nacional de Lugares Históricos).

steps.en: Zoom in until the diamonds appear and click the two nearest your school; the pop-up gives the address.
steps.es: Acércate hasta que aparezcan los rombos y haz clic en los dos más cercanos a tu escuela; la ventana emergente da la dirección.

steps.en: Read the name from the basemap label under the diamond or the pop-up's National Archive Information link.
steps.es: Lee el nombre en la etiqueta del mapa base bajo el rombo o en el enlace National Archive Information de la ventana.

steps.en: Use the legend to tell a building from a district or a site.
steps.es: Usa la leyenda para distinguir un edificio (building) de un distrito (district) o un sitio (site).

ask.en: Is either a public building, such as a courthouse, post office, school or library? Which right or responsibility does it connect with?
ask.es: ¿Alguno es un edificio público, como un tribunal, una oficina de correos, una escuela o una biblioteca? ¿Con qué derecho o responsabilidad se relaciona?

answer.where: National Register of Historic Places layer, on at close zoom. Pop-up: address, city, county, state, resource type and a National Archive Information link; the place name is not shown, so students read it from the basemap label or the National Archives record. Legend: diamond colors for building, structure, district, site and object. If nothing is listed nearby, zoom out to the nearest town.
answer.accept: Two places identified by address or name, with a sensible link for any public building: a courthouse with jury service and a fair trial; a post office or newspaper building with sharing news and ideas; a school or library with staying informed. Accept "neither is a public building" with a reason.

final.teacher: Students answer with evidence from their own map. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, a screenshot of the sketched map with a short caption, or a short talk using the map. Sketches are not saved between sessions.

student.en: Use your map to answer the big question. Choose the three places that best show rights and responsibilities in your community, and explain your choices.
student.es: Usa tu mapa para responder la pregunta central. Elige los tres lugares que mejor muestran los derechos y las responsabilidades en tu comunidad, y explica tu elección.

objectives: Zoom to their own town, click inside their congressional district to read the representative's name, party and district number, and count the districts in their state.
Use the Topographic basemap labels to find four public places in their community and sketch a labelled pin on each with a right from the Bill of Rights that people use there.
Add pins for places where people carry out responsibilities as citizens, and sort those responsibilities into required by law and voluntary.

Turn on the National Register of Historic Places layer, identify the two listed places nearest the school using the pop-up address and the basemap, and connect one public building to a right or responsibility.
Use the places they pinned as evidence to explain where in their community rights and responsibilities are exercised.
discussion: Looking at the pins you sketched, which rights and responsibilities had an obvious building on the basemap and which were hard to place? What does that tell you about where civic life happens?
Your congressional district covers far more than your town. From the pop-up and the district outline, who else shares your representative, and how might their concerns differ from yours?
The National Register diamonds near your school mark places someone decided were worth preserving. Judging from the map, what kinds of places were chosen, and what kinds seem to be missing?

differentiation.support: Zoom to the town from the front and do question 1 together, then give the class three public buildings from the basemap to start their pins.
differentiation.stretch: Click a neighboring district's pop-up and compare representatives and parties, or find a National Register place in another town and explain why it was listed.

resources.title: The Bill of Rights: What Does it Say?

assessment.evidence: Strong answers name places on the student's own map: the representative, party and district number from the Congressional districts (119th Congress) pop-up; public buildings the Topographic basemap labels at close zoom (courthouse, city hall, library, polling place) with the student's Sketch pins; and a National Register of Historic Places diamond identified by its pop-up address and legend type.
assessment.exemplar: In my town, people use their rights and carry out their responsibilities mostly in a few public buildings near the center: the courthouse, the library and the school that serves as a polling place. When I zoomed in on the Topographic basemap until it labeled buildings, I put a Sketch pin on the county courthouse on Main Street, labeled with the right to a jury trial, because that is where trials happen and where people do jury service when called, which is required by law. My second pin is the public library two blocks away, labeled freedom of speech and the press, because anyone can read and share ideas there. My third pin is my school, our polling place, where people vote; voting is a right and a responsibility, but no federal law requires it. The Congressional districts pop-up named my representative, their party and our district number, and when I zoomed out the blue outline covered far more than my town, so my representative speaks for many other places too. With National Register of Historic Places on, the diamond nearest my school had a Main Street address in its pop-up and the legend showed it was a building; the basemap label said it was the old courthouse, so rights have been used in the same place for a long time. One limit is that the map only shows buildings, and some responsibilities, like obeying laws, happen everywhere.

beforeYouStart.en: In 1791, ten amendments, known as the Bill of Rights, were added to the Constitution. They protect rights such as freedom of speech, religion and the press, the right to gather peacefully, and the right to a fair trial. Citizens also have responsibilities to their community and their country.
beforeYouStart.es: En 1791 se añadieron a la Constitución diez enmiendas, conocidas como la Carta de Derechos. Protegen derechos como la libertad de expresión, de religión y de prensa, el derecho a reunirse pacíficamente y el derecho a un juicio justo. Los ciudadanos también tienen responsabilidades con su comunidad y su país.

readingTheMap.en: The Topographic basemap has place names, and labels public buildings when you zoom in close. Blue lines are the boundaries of congressional districts for the 119th Congress (2025–2027); click inside one to see who represents it. National Register of Historic Places is off when the map opens: turn it on in Map layers and zoom in to see its diamonds, colored by type of place (see the legend). Its pop-ups give an address but not a name. Put your pins on public places, not homes. Sketches are not saved when you close the map.
readingTheMap.es: El mapa base Topographic (topográfico) tiene nombres de lugares y muestra los nombres de los edificios públicos cuando te acercas mucho. Las líneas azules son los límites de los distritos del Congreso número 119 (2025–2027); haz clic dentro de uno para ver quién lo representa. La capa National Register of Historic Places está desactivada al abrir el mapa: actívala en las capas del mapa (Map layers) y acércate para ver sus rombos, de colores según el tipo de lugar (mira la leyenda). Sus ventanas emergentes dan una dirección, pero no un nombre. Coloca tus marcadores en lugares públicos, no en viviendas. Los dibujos no se guardan al cerrar el mapa.

reflection.en: What did the map show you about your own community that you hadn't noticed before?
reflection.es: ¿Qué te mostró el mapa sobre tu propia comunidad que no habías notado antes?

teacherNotes.beforeClass: Before class, zoom to your own town and check the basemap labels its public buildings at close zoom. National Register of Historic Places is off when the map opens; its pop-ups give an address but not a name. Students sketch on the map, so remind them sketches are not saved: finish in one session or take a screenshot. Congressional districts and representatives change: check the layer's date before class. Students pin public places only, never homes.

misconceptions.claim: The Bill of Rights lists all of a citizen's rights.
misconceptions.response: The Ninth Amendment says other rights are kept by the people, and later amendments added rights, such as the voting rights in the 15th, 19th and 26th.
No federal law requires it. Serving on a jury when called and paying taxes are required.

misconceptions.claim: Everyone in a state votes for the same representative.
misconceptions.response: Each district elects its own representative; senators are chosen by the whole state.

standards.text: Summarize rights guaranteed in the Bill of Rights
Identify examples of responsible citizenship, including obeying rules and laws, staying informed on public issues, voting, and serving on juries
Analyze how the Bill of Rights guarantees civil rights and liberties to citizens.
Explain specific roles played by citizens (such as voters, jurors, taxpayers, members of the armed forces, petitioners, protesters, and office-holders).
Analyze ideas and principles contained in the founding documents of the United States, and explain how they influence the social and political system.
Construct maps to represent and explain the spatial patterns of cultural and environmental characteristics.
